frase_gancho.texto: The old man who carries the fire of the world.

puente_narrativo.texto: To learn where this god comes from, go to the model of Cuicuilco: the valley’s first great city and the volcano that brought about its end.

guion_corto.texto: In front of you stands one of the first gods of Mesoamerica: Huehuetéotl, the Old God of Fire, made of clay in Cuicuilco, in the south of the valley. He is a hunched old man, seated with his legs crossed and his elbows on his knees, his face lined with wrinkles, with round ear ornaments and his mouth slightly open. On his back he carries a circular vessel, a brazier where embers and copal were burned. It is an image of humility and power at once: the oldest god holds the fire, the center of the universe, and he does so with the weight of centuries. This idea would last more than a thousand years, from Cuicuilco to the Mexica.

guion_largo.texto:
If [the Acrobat](mna_s03_acrobata_tlatilco) spoke of the body, and the split little face spoke of death, the old man in front of you speaks of fire. For the peoples of Mesoamerica, fire was not only warmth and cooking: it was the center of the world, the one that joins the sky with the underworld. That is why its god is an old man. Fire is the oldest and most constant of things, and watching an ember burn in a clay house was a way of being in touch with a force that came from very far back.

This figure came from Cuicuilco, a place where that relationship with fire had more than enough reasons. Cuicuilco grew at the foot of the Xitle volcano, and its people lived, without knowing it, beside a force that would one day destroy them. The Old God of Fire was their way of respecting that force, and of asking it to stay still.

Look at the details. The old man is hunched under the weight of his burden. The wrinkles are made with small strips of clay added with patience: on the forehead, around the eyes, on the cheeks. The ear ornaments are round discs and the mouth is slightly open, missing some teeth. And on his back he carries a vessel shaped like a deep plate, the brazier, where embers and copal resin were burned. In other words: it does not only represent the god of fire, it is also designed to hold fire on top.

Here an image is born that will travel. A thousand years later, in Teotihuacán, Huehuetéotl will be a much larger stone sculpture, with the same gesture, the same brazier and the same wrinkles, and you will see it in the Teotihuacán Hall. And the Mexica called him Xiuhtecuhtli, “Lord of Fire and of Turquoise,” and honored him in a special way every fifty-two years, during the New Fire ceremony: all the fires of the city were put out, and a priest lit a new one at the top of the Hill of the Star, so that the world could go on. From this little clay figure to that ceremony, there is a thread of more than a thousand years.

There is another detail about Cuicuilco that helps us imagine the scene. Today that area is covered with black rock, the Pedregal de San Ángel, which is hardened lava from the Xitle, and on that lava the University City of the UNAM was built. In other words: thousands of students walk every day over the place where the valley’s first great city once stood, and over the volcano that buried it.

That is why this small old man, made of clay, is worth so much. He is small, and that is part of his charm: he fits in one hand, and yet he occupies the center of the universe. He was made by people who knew what lava was, what fire was, what power was. And he is among the first to say it with a human face, old, tired, and at the same time eternal.

texto: Count the wrinkles on the forehead and the cheeks
Find the circular vessel he carries on his back: the brazier
Notice the round ear ornaments and the slightly open mouth

texto.Dimensions: 18 cm high x 16.5 cm in diameter

texto.pregunta: Myth: Huehuetéotl is a Mexica god from the fifteenth century.
texto.respuesta: Reality: This image of the Old God of Fire is much older: it was made in Cuicuilco about two thousand years ago, centuries before the Mexica, who inherited him and called him Xiuhtecuhtli.
